title: Ants! Part 1!
summary: Josh and Chuck open with an announcement that the SketchFest live show in San Francisco has been postponed, then present Part 1 of a two-part episode on ants, Chuck's pick, inspired by listener Joey from Tucson. They cover ant population (roughly a quadrillion), ants' ubiquity (everywhere except Antarctica), their evolutionary ties to wasps and the mud dauber, and collective behavior such as fire ant rafts and army ant bridges built without a leader or plan. They describe ant anatomy (head, mesosoma, petiole, gaster, stingers, mandibles, compound and simple eyes, spiracles), the Schmidt pain scale and bullet ant, the trap jaw ant's jumping bite, and common species (odorous house ant, pavement ant, carpenter ant, red imported fire ant). They discuss ants' omnivorous diet, honeydew and aphid farming, trophallaxis, and slave-making ants. The episode ends by teasing Part 2.

segments.title: SketchFest postponement and episode setup
segments.summary: Chuck announces that the SketchFest live show in San Francisco has been postponed and live shows remain on hold. Josh and Chuck introduce the ants episode, a Chuck pick inspired by listener Joey from Tucson, and preview it as a two-parter.

segments.title: Ant ubiquity, age, and population
segments.summary: The hosts note ants are found on every continent except Antarctica, have existed about 130 million years, and make up a large share of insects in some ecosystems. They estimate roughly a quadrillion ants on Earth and discuss ant biomass compared to humans.

segments.title: Ants and wasps relationship and ecological role
segments.summary: The hosts explain ants are closely related to wasps, with the mud dauber wasp among their close relatives, both in the order Hymenoptera. They describe ants' role in turning soil, moving materials underground, and turning over more soil than earthworms, and note that worker ants are sterile females with stingers.

segments.title: Fire ant rafts
segments.summary: Red imported fire ants link together into waterproof, buoyant rafts when dropped in water. Researcher work at Georgia Tech is mentioned, describing how ants interlock and push apart to trap air, with no leader or brain-held plan.

segments.title: Army ant bridges and collective intelligence
segments.summary: Nomadic army ants form living bridges across gaps, supporting the weight of traffic and disassembling afterward. The hosts marvel that ants have no leader or blueprint and say humans still do not fully understand how colonies coordinate.

segments.title: Common North American ant species
segments.summary: The hosts describe the odorous house ant (sugar ant, coconut ant), the pavement ant, and the carpenter ant, which is large and not venomous. Chuck recounts being stung after standing in a pile of fire ants shortly after moving south.

segments.title: Ant anatomy: head, mandibles, eyes, and body segments
segments.summary: The hosts describe the ant head with antennae used for pheromone sensing, compound and simple eyes, and mandibles. They discuss the bullet ant and Schmidt pain scale, and the trap jaw ant's fast jumping bite. They then move through the mesosoma, petiole, and gaster, which holds the heart and stinger and breathes via spiracles.

segments.title: Ant strength and exoskeleton
segments.summary: The hosts explain that ants have a chitin exoskeleton that withstands large forces and muscles with high cross-sectional area, letting some carry around fifty times their body weight.

segments.title: Ant diet, honeydew, and aphid farming
segments.summary: The hosts describe ants as omnivores that eat flesh, nectar, and other insects. They explain how ants tend aphids, herding them and protecting them from ladybugs to harvest honeydew, and describe trophallaxis, the sharing of food between ants.

segments.title: Slave-making ants
segments.summary: The hosts describe slave-making ant species that raid closely related colonies, capture workers, and force them to labor in their own colony.

segments.title: Part 1 wrap-up and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up Part 1, note there is no listener mail this week, preview Part 2 on Thursday, and give the contact email and credits.
